title: Mycosis fungoides & cutaneous lymphoma
summary: The commonest cutaneous lymphoma: fixed, slowly changing eczema- or psoriasis-like patches in sun-protected sites that do not settle with treatment. Most patients have early-stage disease with a normal life expectancy.

glance.think: Persistent, scaly, salmon-pink patches or thin plaques on the buttocks, hips, trunk or breasts that ‘never quite clear’ despite steroids.
glance.engine: Skin-homing clonal helper T cells; progresses slowly from patch to plaque to tumour; Sézary syndrome is the leukaemic form with erythroderma.
glance.backbone: Suspect, stop repeated empirical treatment, refer for multiple biopsies; specialist skin-directed therapy (steroids, phototherapy) for early disease.
glance.never_miss: Tumour-stage disease, erythroderma with lymph nodes (Sézary), misdiagnosis as eczema or psoriasis for years.

what: **MF is the commonest primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL)**, about half of all primary cutaneous lymphomas. It is usually indolent over years to decades, with a minority progressing. **Sézary syndrome** is the leukaemic, erythrodermic variant.
cause: Clonal skin-homing CD4+ memory T-cells (CD4+, often CD7- and CD26-). Cause unknown; links to chronic antigen stimulation have been proposed. **Pautrier microabscesses** (intraepidermal collections of atypical lymphocytes) and **epidermotropism** without spongiosis are the histological hallmark, but they are absent in many early biopsies.

list: **Patch stage:** persistent, variably shaped, often **finely wrinkled ("cigarette-paper") pink-brown patches in sun-protected "bathing-trunk" sites** (buttocks, hips, breasts, inner thighs). Itchy or asymptomatic, **steroid-resistant or relapsing**.

**Erythroderma**, poikiloderma (atrophy, mottled pigmentation, telangiectasia), and variants (folliculotropic, hypopigmented in skin of colour and children, granulomatous slack skin, pagetoid reticulosis).
**Multiple biopsies** (ideally after a 2–4-week washout of topical steroids) with immunohistochemistry and **TCR gene rearrangement** (clonality). Diagnosis often takes years.

**ISCL/EORTC algorithm for early MF**. Diagnosis needs **≥4 points**: **Clinical:** 2 points for the basic criterion (persistent and/or progressive patches/plaques) plus 2 of the additional criteria (non-sun-exposed distribution; size or shape variation; poikiloderma), or 1 point for the basic criterion plus 1 additional; **Histopathology:** 2 points for a superficial lymphoid infiltrate plus both epidermotropism without spongiosis and lymphoid atypia, or 1 point for the infiltrate plus one of those; **Molecular:** clonal TCR rearrangement = 1 point; **Immunopathology:** CD2/3/5 <50% of T-cells, CD7 <10%, or epidermal/dermal discordance = 1 point

list: Staging investigations (specialist): FBC + blood film/flow cytometry for Sézary cells, LDH, LFTs, HTLV-1 serology, and CT (or PET-CT) for stage ≥IIA or as indicated. Biopsy suspicious nodes.

differentials: **Chronic eczema (including occupational contact dermatitis, relevant to a mechanic; patch test)**, psoriasis, tinea corporis (scrape), parapsoriasis (small- and large-plaque, where large-plaque can progress), pityriasis lichenoides, **drug-induced pseudolymphoma / MF-like drug eruptions** (reported with, among others, anticonvulsants, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, **amlodipine** and other calcium-channel blockers, and dupilumab-associated CTCL unmasking), lichen planus, cutaneous lupus.

list: A **rash not responding to an appropriate potent topical steroid over several weeks, especially in sun-protected sites, should be referred for biopsy**. Do not repeat or escalate steroids indefinitely, as happened for 12 months in [Case 5](condition:basal-cell-carcinoma). Refer **routinely to urgently depending on stage clues** (tumours, erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, systemic symptoms: urgent). Primary cutaneous lymphoma is managed in **specialist supra-network skin lymphoma MDTs**.

Review drug triggers. Stopping a suspected culprit (e.g. amlodipine) and reviewing after 6–12 weeks may be appropriate *before or alongside* biopsy. This is a joint decision with the GP/dermatologist.

[Case 5](condition:basal-cell-carcinoma) medicines: **canagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor)** has no link to MF but carries genital mycotic infection and DKA risk (check the patient's wellbeing). Metformin: none. Simvastatin + amlodipine: the BNF/MHRA cap simvastatin at **20 mg** with amlodipine (CYP3A4 interaction), so check the dose.

**Early (IA–IIA): skin-directed therapy.** Potent/very potent topical steroid; **phototherapy** (narrowband UVB for patches, PUVA for thicker plaques; the course answer); topical **chlormethine gel** (Ledaga®); localised radiotherapy; topical bexarotene (not UK-licensed); and for many IA patients, "expectant" skin-directed care.

**Advanced (IIB–IV):** Total-skin electron beam therapy; Systemic **bexarotene** (hypertriglyceridaemia and central hypothyroidism; needs a lipid-lowering agent and levothyroxine; **avoid gemfibrozil**); Low-dose **methotrexate**; Interferon-α; **Mogamulizumab** (anti-CCR4; NICE TA754: Sézary after ≥1 systemic therapy, MF stage IIB+ after ≥2); **Brentuximab vedotin** for CD30+ (NICE TA577); Extracorporeal photopheresis (Sézary); Chemotherapy; Allogeneic stem-cell transplant in selected patients
Quality of life: **itch** (emollients, antihistamines, gabapentin/pregabalin, mirtazapine, aprepitant for refractory itch), and work and psychological impact.

Subcutaneous panniculitis-like TCL; primary cutaneous γδ TCL (aggressive); adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (**HTLV-1**); extranodal NK/T-cell (nasal type)
Primary cutaneous **marginal zone** and **follicle centre** lymphoma (indolent: head/trunk nodules); **diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, leg type** (older women, red nodules on the leg; aggressive)

red_flags: Fixed patches or plaques in sun-protected sites that fail to respond to treatment over months: refer for **biopsy** (MF).
Erythroderma with lymph nodes, intense itch and weight loss: **urgent** referral (Sézary syndrome).
pearls: Explain that early MF is usually a **chronic, indolent** condition (stage IA has near-normal life expectancy). Avoid the "advanced cancer" framing without staging.
Cumulative UV raises skin cancer risk.
**Dupilumab caveat:** CTCL has been unmasked or accelerated in patients misdiagnosed with atopic dermatitis. In an atypical adult-onset "eczema" that is failing treatment, biopsy before biologics.
